effects.title: Sink {villain}'s Flagship
effects.text: The reaver {villain} raids the coast of {kingdom}. Sink the flagship and the fleet will scatter.

daily.text: Reavers came ashore at {target} by night.

actions.label: Pay {villain} to raid elsewhere
actions.text: A purse of gold goes out to the flagship in a rowing boat. {villain}'s answer comes back: a bow, and a promise to sail for richer coasts.

actions.label: Fund the royal fleet of {kingdom}
actions.text: Your gold buys pitch, timber and crews for the royal fleet. Its admiral salutes you.

sea_battle.title: The Battle of the Headland
sea_battle.text: The royal fleet of {kingdom} sails out to meet {villain} off {settlement}. For two days the smoke of burning ships hangs over the water.
sea_battle.rumor: The king's ships have gone out against {villain}. Every widow in {settlement} is on the cliffs.

reavers_broken.title: The Flagship Burns
reavers_broken.text: {villain}'s flagship goes down in flames, and the reaver fleet scatters like crows from a gunshot. Bells ring in every harbour of {kingdom}.

effects.chronicle: {house} sank the flagship of the reaver {villain} off {settlement}.

reavers_bought.title: Paid to Go
reavers_bought.text: {villain} takes the gold and sails away — to raid some other coast with ships your silver repaired. The harbours of {kingdom} reopen; elsewhere, others pay.

effects.name: Emboldened Reavers
effects.text: Paid-off reavers roam the seas.

effects.chronicle: {house} paid the reaver {villain} to leave the coast of {kingdom}.

crown_victory.title: The Crown's Victory
crown_victory.text: The royal fleet of {kingdom} breaks the reavers. {villain} is hanged from the yardarm of their own flagship, and the admiral is the hero of the hour.

effects.chronicle: {house} paid for the ships that broke the reaver {villain}.

reaver_coast.title: The Reaver Coast
reaver_coast.text: The royal fleet is beaten. {villain} styles themself Lord of the Reaver Coast, and every ship that passes {settlement} pays toll or burns.

effects.name: The Reaver Coast
effects.text: {villain} rules the sea-lanes off {kingdom}.

effects.chronicle: The beacon-watch {house} raised kept the reavers of {villain} from its own shores.

sundering_faith.name: The Sundering Faith
sundering_faith.summary: A barefoot preacher is splitting the faith of {kingdom} in two.

council.title: Which Altar?
council.text: Two delegations wait in your hall: the bishop's clerks with a writ against the new preaching, and a crowd of the preacher's followers with a petition of their own. Each wants your name on their side.

ignore.result: You signed nothing. Both sides took it as an insult.

choices.label: Sign the bishops' writ
choices.result: The preacher's followers are turned out of your chapels.

choices.label: Sign the reformers' petition
choices.result: The reformers cheer your name in the streets. The bishop does not.

choices.label: Sign neither, and call for a council
choices.result: You pay for a hall and a feast. Both sides come, if only to argue.

preacher.title: The Barefoot Preacher
preacher.text: {villain} walks barefoot into {settlement} and preaches against the gold of the {faith} bishops. Thousands come to hear; the bishops call it the {heresy}.
preacher.rumor: There's a preacher called {villain} in {settlement} telling folk the bishops have sold {faith} for gold.

actions.label: Hear {villain} preach
actions.text: You stand in the crowd. {villain} speaks plainly and well — and much of it is true.

schism.title: Schism
schism.text: The council of {kingdom} splits. Half the lords take {villain}'s side; the bishops excommunicate them all. In {kingdom2}, the faithful of {faith} watch and choose sides.
schism.rumor: {kingdom} is split over {villain}. A council could heal it — if anyone had the standing to call one.

effects.name: Schism
effects.text: Schism tears at the faith of {kingdom}.

effects.title: Heal the Schism
effects.text: The faith of {kingdom} is splitting over {villain}. Call a council of reconciliation, or see one side win.

actions.label: Champion {villain}'s reforms
actions.text: You declare for the reformers. {villain} embraces you before the crowd.

actions.label: Stand with the bishops
actions.text: You kneel to the bishops and swear to defend the old order. Your men are at their disposal.

actions.label: Call a council of reconciliation
actions.text: You pay for the great hall, the feast and the guards, and you sit at the head of the table while bishops and reformers shout at each other for nine days. On the tenth, they agree.

strife.title: Holy Strife
strife.text: Mobs of reformers and loyalists fight in the streets of {settlement}. Churches burn; {kingdom2} sends priests and silver to the bishops, and relations between the realms sour.
strife.rumor: They're burning churches in {settlement}. {kingdom2} is backing the bishops.

effects.name: Holy Strife
effects.text: Holy strife burns in {kingdom}.

actions.label: Force a truce between the factions
actions.text: With your soldiers between the mobs and your gold in the bishops' coffers, a truce is sworn on the cathedral steps.

reconciled.title: The Council of Reconciliation
reconciled.text: Bishops and reformers kneel side by side. The worst of the bishops' gold goes to the poor; {villain} is made an abbot and told to stop walking barefoot. {kingdom} is whole again.

effects.chronicle: {house} healed the schism of {kingdom} at the Council of Reconciliation.

reformed.title: The Reformation
reformed.text: The reformers win. The bishops' palaces are sold, {villain} is hailed a saint in their own lifetime, and the faith of {kingdom} is plainer, poorer, and fiercer.

effects.chronicle: {house} stood with {villain} and the reformers of {kingdom}, and won.

orthodoxy.title: The Bonfire
orthodoxy.text: The bishops win. {villain} is burned in the square at {settlement} and the {heresy} is driven underground, where it will smoulder for a generation.

effects.chronicle: {house} stood with the bishops of {kingdom} when {villain} was burned.

iron_company.name: The Iron Company
iron_company.summary: The unpaid sellswords of {kingdom} are turning on their masters.

tolls.title: Tolls on the King's Road
tolls.text: Merchants complain that sellswords of the Iron Company have set up a toll-chain on the road to your gates and take a tenth of every cart. They want an escort, or a lord with the stomach to clear the road.

ignore.result: The merchants paid the toll, and charged you for it in their prices.

choices.label: Hire escorts for the merchant carts
choices.result: Carts move under your guards' spears. The sellswords watch, and let them pass.

choices.label: Pay the Company to lift the chain
choices.result: The chain comes down. For now.

choices.label: Raise a levy to clear the road
choices.result: Your levy marches out with pitchforks and old spears. The toll-chain is gone by evening.

unpaid.title: Wages in Arrears
unpaid.text: The Iron Company — three hundred sellswords in the pay of {kingdom} — have not been paid since the spring. Their captain, {villain}, has begun to speak of 'taking wages in kind'.
unpaid.rumor: The Iron Company's men are drinking on credit in {settlement}. {villain} says the crown owes them, and they'll collect.

actions.label: Pay the Company's arrears yourself
actions.text: You count out the Company's back-pay on a drumhead. {villain} bites a coin, grins, and swears the Company to your name.

rogue.title: The Company Goes Rogue
rogue.text: The Iron Company tears up its contract. {villain} leads three hundred veterans out of {settlement}, chaining roads, burning the farms of anyone who will not pay, and daring the crown of {kingdom} to stop them.
rogue.rumor: The Iron Company has turned bandit around {settlement}. {villain} will take a new contract — at a price.

effects.name: The Free Company
effects.text: The Iron Company plunders {kingdom}.

effects.title: Break the Iron Company
effects.text: The rogue Iron Company plunders {kingdom}. Beat them in the field, or buy their swords.

effects.news: {rival} has been seen drinking with {villain}'s officers.

actions.label: Buy the Company's contract
actions.text: You meet {villain} in a burned farmhouse. The price is steep, but three hundred veterans will march under your banner — for a while.

sack.title: The Sack of {settlement}
sack.text: The Iron Company storms {settlement}. For three days they loot it street by street; the crown of {kingdom} pays a ransom to make them leave.
sack.rumor: {settlement} has been sacked by the Iron Company. They're heading for the border with {kingdom2}.

broken.title: The Company Broken
broken.text: The Iron Company is broken in the field. {villain} dies with a sword in hand; the survivors scatter or sign on with honest masters. The roads of {kingdom} open again.

effects.chronicle: {house} broke the Iron Company and slew its captain, {villain}.

company_hired.title: A New Paymaster
company_hired.text: The Iron Company has a new paymaster, and it is you. {villain} keeps the Company in good order; {kingdom} breathes again and wonders what you mean to do with three hundred swords.

effects.chronicle: {house} bought the swords of the Iron Company and its captain, {villain}.

broken_by_crown.title: The King's Justice
broken_by_crown.text: The Iron Company is cut down by the crown's soldiers. {villain}'s head goes up over the gate of {settlement}.

moves_on.title: Over the Border
moves_on.text: Rich with plunder, the Iron Company crosses into {kingdom2}. Each court blames the other for letting them pass.

effects.name: The Free Company
effects.text: The Iron Company plunders {kingdom2}.

the_comet.name: The Comet
the_comet.summary: A comet with a forked tail hangs over the world, and a seer reads doom in it.

omen.title: The Forked Star
omen.text: A comet with a forked tail hangs in the night sky, brighter every evening. Astrologers argue; farmers bury coins at the crossroads for luck.
omen.rumor: Have you seen the star with two tails? The priests of {faith} say it is a warning.

effects.name: The Forked Star
effects.text: A forked comet hangs in the sky.

actions.label: Pay an astrologer to chart the comet
actions.text: Your astrologer works out the comet's path with brass and patience. It will pass, she says — and a piece of it may already have fallen, near {settlement}.

prophecy.title: The Prophecy
prophecy.text: {villain}, a seer of {settlement}, prophesies that when the comet turns red the line of {ruler} will end. A cult gathers to wait for the day; they call themselves the {heresy}.
prophecy.rumor: {villain} says the comet will turn red and {ruler}'s line will end. They say a piece of the star fell near {settlement}.

effects.name: Star Cult
effects.text: A star cult waits for doom in {kingdom}.

effects.title: The Riddle of the Comet
effects.text: {villain} prophesies doom for {kingdom}. Find what fell from the sky near {settlement}, or prove the seer wrong.
effects.objective: Solve the riddle of the comet

actions.label: Debate {villain} before the cult
actions.text: You lay your astrologer's charts before the crowd: the comet's colour is the dust of its tail, and it will pass in a month. {villain} has no answer.

reddening.title: The Red Star
reddening.text: The comet turns red as blood. Panic in {kingdom}: the cult dances in the streets of {settlement}, merchants hoard, and {ruler} doubles the guard.
reddening.rumor: The comet's gone red. The cult of {villain} says the end is days away.

effects.name: The Red Star
effects.text: Panic grips {kingdom} under a red star.

actions.label: Debate {villain} before the cult
actions.text: Even under a red sky, your charts carry the day. The comet is already fading.

starfall.title: The Star-Iron
starfall.text: In the crater lies a lump of black star-iron, warm to the touch. Displayed in {settlement}, it shows the comet for what it is: a stone from the sky. The cult of {villain} melts away.

effects.chronicle: {house} found the star-iron that fell with the Forked Comet.

debunked.title: The Seer Confounded
debunked.text: {villain} is laughed out of {settlement}. The comet fades from the sky on the night you predicted, and astrologers across {kingdom} quote your charts.

effects.chronicle: {house} confounded the seer {villain} and charted the Forked Comet.

cult_rises.title: The Cult of the Red Star
cult_rises.text: The comet fades, but the cult does not. {villain}'s followers say the doom was only delayed, and their numbers grow in {kingdom}.

fades.title: The Star Fades
fades.text: The comet fades. Nothing falls, no line ends. {villain} quietly leaves {settlement}, and in a year no one admits to having believed.

discovery._comment: Uncharted lands (src/systems/discovery.js): remote islands, hidden coves, lost valleys and sunken reefs chosen lazily from the generated map by a hash of the world seed; how they are found, named, sold, settled and contested; the exotic goods found there (merged into playerEconomy GOODS at load, never stocked by any market).

goods.name: Ambergris
goods.description: Grey treasure of the whale roads, worth its weight in silver to perfumers.

goods.name: Pearls
goods.description: Lustrous pearls from untouched oyster beds.

goods.name: Sea Silk
goods.description: Golden thread spun from the beards of giant shellfish.

goods.name: Cloudpepper
goods.description: A fiery spice that grows nowhere on any known shore.

goods.name: Blue Coral
goods.description: Coral the colour of deep water, prized by jewellers.

goods.name: Ghost Orchid
goods.description: A pale orchid from hidden valleys; physicians and princes pay dearly.

goods.name: Golden Amber
goods.description: Amber holding the insects of a vanished age.

rumours: Fishermen in {town} swear they saw birds of a kind no one knows, flying out of the {dir}.
A drunk sailor in {town} talks of a {kind} somewhere to the {dir}, about {leagues} leagues off.
An old trapper in {town} claims there is a {kind} beyond the wild country to the {dir}.
Driftwood carved by unknown hands washes up near {town}. It comes from the {dir}.

famine_relief.title: Food for {town}
famine_relief.text: {issuer} pays well for food delivered to {town}, where the granaries run low.

siege_relief.title: Relieve {town}
siege_relief.text: {issuer} will pay a war premium for supplies run into {town} while the enemy is at the walls.

fleet_timber.title: Timber for the Fleet
fleet_timber.text: The royal shipwrights of {issuer} need {good} at {town} to build and refit the fleet.

war_iron.title: Iron for the War
war_iron.text: {issuer}'s armouries at {town} want {good} for the war.

walls_stone.title: Stone for the Walls
walls_stone.text: The masons of {town} are raising new walls for {issuer} and need {good}.

court_luxuries.title: A Court Wedding
court_luxuries.text: {issuer}'s court celebrates at {town} and orders {good} for the feast.

ventures.name: Spice Fleet to the Far Isles
ventures.text: {kingdom} fits out a fleet for the spice islands and sells shares in the cargo.

ventures.name: The Northern Whaling Voyage
ventures.text: {kingdom}'s whalers sail north and want investors for the oil.

ventures.name: The Crown Silver Mine
ventures.text: {kingdom} opens a deep silver working and offers shares in the first seams.

ventures.name: The Long Caravan East
ventures.text: {kingdom} sends a great caravan over the eastern passes and sells shares in what it brings back.

kingship._comment: Kingship — ruling a realm as its sovereign (src/systems/kingship.js, built on systems/throne.js). The royal council's great offices, realm-wide edicts with upkeep, the realm's lords as vassals (opinion, ambition, power, factions, levy refusal and revolt), and the AI's regard for a player-ruled realm. Office and edict 'mods' are kingdom bonus keys (world/kingdomState.js KingdomBonuses) fed through kingdom.crown.mods; office mods are per point of competence (1-20), scaled by the councillor's loyalty.

revolt._holdingSacked: A rebel host that storms one of the player's own holdings sacks it (unrest, garrison and people lost); it never becomes a rebel seat.

chancellor.label: Chancellor
chancellor.blurb: Foreign affairs: warmer envoys, better odds of peace, and one more edict the court can manage at 12+ competence.

marshal.label: Marshal
marshal.blurb: The royal host: armies rebuild faster and the realm keeps a larger one.

steward.label: Steward
steward.blurb: The royal treasury: more income for the crown. A disloyal steward skims.

spymaster.label: Spymaster
spymaster.blurb: Plots revealed: vassal factions come to light before they strike, and rebellion is rooted out.

highPriest.label: High Priest
highPriest.blurb: Faith unity: the realm's church draws together (and steadies the realm).

conscription.label: Conscription
conscription.blurb: Every village sends its sons. A larger, faster-mustering host; the commons and the lords' fields suffer.

road_programme.label: Road-building programme
road_programme.blurb: Royal surveyors and corvée gangs pave the king's highways. Trade and building quicken, and roads and bridges you build in the realm cost 40% less.

tolerance.label: Religious tolerance
tolerance.blurb: Every people may keep its rites. Minorities settle; the bishops fume and the church frays a little.

persecution.label: Persecution of heretics
persecution.blurb: Inquisitors ride. The faith hardens and unites; minorities seethe.

merchant_charters.label: Merchant charters
merchant_charters.blurb: Free towns and guild charters. Trade booms; the crown's dues are lighter, and a company charter from the realm costs half.

famine_dole.label: Famine dole
famine_dole.blurb: Royal granaries open to the hungry. In the lean weeks and in famine the crown ships grain to every town short of stores — paid from the treasury by the cartload — easing hunger, unrest and the famine's toll on the people. In good times it costs little.

royal_post.label: The Royal Post
royal_post.blurb: One courier house is granted the realm's mail: no other may carry a letter from its towns. Its weekly fee — so much a station — comes to the royal treasury (the demesne line of the crown's books). Name the house when you proclaim it; change the holder or revoke it at will. A grant your predecessor made stands as this edict until you revoke it.

crown_monopolies.label: Crown monopolies
crown_monopolies.blurb: Salt, iron and wine — and the tools, weapons and liquor made from them — are the crown's alone. Every town of the realm sells them only through the crown's factors, 30% dearer, and the markup goes to the royal treasury; no trading company may deal in them there. Merchants and greedy lords resent it, and rival merchant houses earn less from their posts in the realm.

royal_assizes.label: Royal assizes
royal_assizes.blurb: The king's judges ride circuit and overrule the lords' own courts. Order and loyalty — and baronial grumbling.

scutage.label: Scutage
scutage.blurb: The lords pay gold instead of knight-service. A richer crown, a smaller host, and lords who keep their men at home.

patronage.label: Royal patronage of the arts
patronage.blurb: Poets, painters and scholars at court. Learning and renown spread; foreign courts admire you.

fortification.label: Fortification of the marches
fortification.blurb: Stone castles on every border. The realm is harder to take, and your own holdings in it hold out behind stronger walls.

counsel._comment: The Steward's Counsel (src/systems/counsel.js): the advisor's rules. Each rule names a reader (Counsel.READERS) that returns facts; the fact fields fill the {placeholders} in 'text'. group: threat | opportunity | goal. severity: critical | warning | notice | info (a fact may override it). priority orders items of equal severity (a fact may add a 'boost'). panel: the ActionMenu panel the item's button opens (ui/actionMenu/counsel.js COUNSEL_PANELS); items with a map hex also get a 'show on map' button. params: per-rule tunables passed to the reader. max: items kept per rule (config.maxPerRule otherwise). heavy: whole-world scans, read at most once a day. enabled:false switches a rule off.

chatter._comment: A living world: what townsfolk say about what is happening (systems/chatter.js), the heralds' proclamations (systems/heralds.js) and the tavern's regional news (player/tavern/intel.js). Line groups are chosen by conditions on world and player state; see the manual, 'Townsfolk Talk & Heralds'.

underwriter_failed: Hear ye! {uw} of {place} cannot meet its claims and has shut its doors. Its policies are void.
{uw} is broken: too many ships lost, too many claims. Merchants of {place}, look to your cover.
great_claim: {uw} pays {amount} gold on a single claim. The underwriters of {place} grumble over their ledgers.
A great loss is made good: {uw} of {place} pays out {amount} gold.
insured_catastrophe: A great storm has sunk a fleet insured at {place}. {uw} must pay {amount} gold.
Ill news for {uw}: a whole fleet lost, and {amount} gold of claims to meet.
bourse_mania: All {place} buys {listing}! Its shares double while you sleep, they say.
A fever for {listing} grips the Bourse of {place}. Cobblers sell their lasts to buy a share.
bourse_crash: Hear ye! {listing} has crashed at the Bourse of {place}. Fortunes made in a season are gone in a morning.
The bubble is burst: {listing} falls by half at {place}, and {bank} counts its losses.
bourse_panic: Panic at the Bourse of {place}! Every share falls as the news of {bank} spreads.
The floor at {place} is in uproar: sellers and no buyers.
mine_strike: Hear ye! A new {site} is struck in the hills near {place}. Miners and carters, there is work to be had!
Strike! The prospectors of {place} have found a {site}; {good} will come down from the hills before the season is out.
By leave of the crown of {kingdom}, a {site} is opened near {place}. Let honest men go dig.
estate_enclosure: Hear ye! {holder} has hedged the fields of {estate} near {place} and put them to sheep. {n} households are turned out and go to {to}.
Sheep eat men at {place}: {holder} encloses {estate}, and {n} families take the road to {to}.
estate_riot: Riot at {place}! The cottagers of {estate} have torn down {holder}'s hedges and beaten the bailiff.
The peasants of {estate} near {place} have risen against {holder}. The sheriff's men ride out.
estate_sold: {holder} has sold {estate} near {place} to {buyer} for {price} gold.
Land for sale no more: {estate} near {place} passes from {holder} to {buyer}, for {price} gold.
estate_confiscated: By right of conquest {buyer} takes {estate} near {place}, the land of {holder}.
The new masters of {place} seize {estate} from {holder}.
estate_ceded: By the terms of peace, {holder} cedes {estate} near {place} to {buyer}.
{estate} near {place} is given up to {buyer}: the price of a lost war for {holder}.
estate_bequest: {holder} has left {estate} near {place} to {buyer}, for the good of his soul.
By the will of {holder}, the Church takes {estate} near {place}. Its tenants pay their rent to the abbey now.
estate_dowry: {estate} near {place} goes with a bride: {holder} settles it on {buyer} as a dowry.
A marriage between noble houses of {kingdom}: {buyer} has {estate} near {place} from {holder}, as the bride's portion.
estate_rent_riot: Riot at {place}! The tenants of {estate} have risen against {holder} over the rent, and the bailiff is beaten.
No rent at {estate} near {place} this month, only cudgels: the tenants of {holder} will not pay what is asked.
grain_engrossed: The harvest is failing in {kingdom}, and the grain dealers are buying it up: {amount} loads gone into their lofts. Bread will be dear.
Engrossers in {kingdom}! The dealers hoard grain against the hungry months, and the price climbs already.
engrossing_edict: By order of the crown of {kingdom}: no man shall hoard grain. The dealers' lofts at {place} are thrown open; {amount} grain comes to market.
The crown of {kingdom} forbids engrossing! The hoarders of {place} must sell, and bread is cheaper by nightfall.
linen_glut: Linen is cheap in {kingdom}: the cottage looms have flooded the markets of {place} and {n} towns besides.
The cottagers of {kingdom} weave more linen than the realm can wear: it goes for a song at {place}.
mine_vein: The old {site} near {place} has found a fresh vein: the pits will not close this year.
Good news from {place}: a new seam in the {site}, and {good} enough for years yet.
mine_exhausted: Hear ye! The {site} near {place} is worked out and its pits are shut. {good} will be dear hereabouts.
The last cart of {good} has come down from the {site} near {place}. Its miners take the road to {to}.
No more {good} from the hills of {place}: the {site} is dug out, and the price has gone up already.
mine_accident: Woe at {place}! A gallery has fallen in at the {site}: {n} miners are dead.
A fall at the {site} near {place} has killed {n}. The town blames the masters, who drive the men too hard.
guild_strike: Hear ye! The {guild} has downed tools over {reason}. There will be little {good} in {place} for {days} days.
The masters of the {guild} have shut their shops: {reason}, they say. Whoever brings {good} to {place} will sell it dear.
Strike at {place}! {master} and the {guild} will not work until the crown of {kingdom} hears them.
guild_election: The masters of the {guild} have chosen {master} to lead them.
Hear ye! {master} is guildmaster of the {guild} at {place}.
guild_chartered: By royal charter, the {guild} alone may set the trade of {place}. {master} gives thanks to the crown of {kingdom}.
Hear ye! The crown of {kingdom} grants the {guild} its charter, and its masters their privileges.
guild_abolished: Hear ye! The {guild} is broken by order of the crown. Any man may now work its trade in {place}.
The guildhall at {place} is shut and its charter burned: the {guild} is no more.
trade_embargo: Hear ye! By order of the crown of {kingdom}, no goods of {other} may be bought or sold in its markets.
The crown of {kingdom} closes its roads and harbours to the merchants of {other}. Smugglers rejoice.
Embargo! {kingdom} will have no trade with {other} until the crown says otherwise.
trade_treaty: Hear ye! {kingdom} and {other} sign a treaty of trade: no duties between them, and safe roads for their merchants.
The seals are set: the merchants of {kingdom} and {other} may cross each other's borders without paying a copper.
A treaty of commerce between {kingdom} and {other}! The carters cheer and the toll-keepers sulk.
trade_war: Hear ye! {kingdom} raises its duties on the goods of {other}, in answer to {other}'s own.
Duty upon duty: {kingdom} and {other} are at war over tariffs, and the merchants pay for both.
The customs men of {kingdom} have new orders: every cart from {other} pays dearer at the border.
trade_ban: Hear ye! While the realm goes hungry, no {good} may leave {kingdom}, by order of the crown.
The crown of {kingdom} bans the sale of {good} across its borders. Let our own be fed first!
No {good} out of {kingdom}: the border posts are turning the wagons back.
trade_granary: Hear ye! The royal granaries of {kingdom} are opened: {n} measures of grain for the hungry towns.
The crown of {kingdom} feeds its people from the royal stores. Bless the good years that filled them!
Grain carts from the royal granaries roll into the hungry towns of {kingdom}. No one starves this season.
econ_dear: Hear ye! Bread is dear in {kingdom}: food costs {pct}% more than in {since}. The crown's criers bid the carters make haste.
The criers of {kingdom} cry the price of bread: up {pct}% since {since}, and the poor feel it first.
Dear bread in {kingdom}! Food fetches {food}% of its worth, {pct}% more than in {since}. Grain bought cheap elsewhere will sell well there.
econ_inflation: Hear ye! Prices in {kingdom} have climbed {pct}% since {since}. The goodwives blame the bakers, the bakers blame the coin.
The criers of {kingdom} confess it: everything costs {pct}% more than it did in {since}.
Prices rise in {kingdom}: {pct}% since {since}. A purse of silver buys less each week.
road_washout: Hear ye! The bridge on the road from {place} to {other} is swept away by the flood; {crossing} until it is built again.
The river has taken the bridge between {place} and {other}. Carters wait at the water's edge; {crossing}.
pass_closed: Hear ye! Snow has shut the pass between {place} and {other}. No carts will cross before the thaw.
The road over the mountains from {place} to {other} lies under snow. Traders turn back; prices on the far side will climb.
highway_opened: Hear ye! {kingdom} has paved the road from {place} to {other}: a highway now, wagons roll in half the time.
The new highway between {place} and {other} is open. Merchants of {kingdom}, rejoice: cheaper carriage, swifter trade.
bridge_built: Hear ye! A stone bridge now carries the road from {place} to {other} over the river.
The masons are done: the bridge between {place} and {other} stands. No more fording, no more waiting for the ferry.
canal_opened: Hear ye! The canal from {place} to {other} is open: barges glide where carts once laboured.
Water joins {place} and {other} at last. The new canal carries grain and stone at a fraction of the old cost.
harbour_built: Hear ye! The harbour works of {place} are finished: new quays, deeper berths, cheaper freight by sea.
{place} has its new harbour. Ships load faster there now, and the sea trade of {kingdom} will grow.
harvest_failing: Hear ye! The harvest in {place} is failing: the fields promise barely {pct}% of a common year. Lay in grain while it is cheap.
Ill news from {place}: the crop withers in the fields, {pct}% of a fair harvest at best. Bread will be dear there by spring.
The reeves of {place} send word: a thin harvest is coming, {pct}% of the usual. The granaries will be wanted.
harvest_bumper: Hear ye! The fields of {place} stand heavy: a bumper harvest is coming, {pct}% of a common year. Grain will be cheap there.
Good news from {place}: the finest crop in memory ripens, {pct}% of the usual. The brewers rejoice.
harvest_blight: Hear ye! {blight} is in the fields of {place}. The farmers burn what they cannot save.
Woe to {place}: {blight} has come, out of {from}. Pray it stops at the river.
The criers of {place} bid all to watch their fields and herds: {blight} is abroad.
harvest_poor: Hear ye! The harvest of {place} is in, and it is poor: {pct}% of a common year. Hard months lie ahead.
The last sheaves are in at {place}: a lean harvest, {pct}% of the usual. The bakers have raised their prices already.
harvest_plenty: Hear ye! A rich harvest is gathered in {place}: {pct}% of a common year. The barns overflow and grain goes cheap.
Plenty in {place}! The harvest came in at {pct}% of the usual; the brewers and the poor alike give thanks.
fashion: Hear ye! At the court of {place}, {text}: {goods} fetch a premium wherever the fashion reaches.
News from {place}: {text}. Whoever has {goods} to sell should make for the courts.
The criers bring word from {place}: {text}, and the merchants scramble for {goods}.
labour_refugees: Hear ye! {n} souls have fled {place} for fear of {why}, and crowd the roads to {to}. Charity, good people!
The roads out of {place} are thick with carts and bundles: {n} have fled the {why} for {to} and the towns beyond.
By order of the crown of {kingdom}: let {to} open its gates to the folk of {place}, who flee the {why}.
labour_strike: Hear ye! The artisans of {place} have downed their tools: their wages buy no bread. The workshops stand cold for {days} days.
The guilds of {place} are out in the square, not at the bench: bread is dear and the masters pay the old rate.
No hammer rings in {place}: its craftsmen strike against the price of bread.
labour_boom: Hear ye! {place} prospers: work for every hand and bread on every table, and newcomers arrive by the cartload.
Times are good in {place}: the workshops hire, the stalls are full and folk are flocking in from the villages.
{place} is the place to be, say the carters: good wages, full larders and a roof for all who come.
market_fair: Hear ye! The {fair} is open in {place} for {days} days. Merchants from far lands, and every stall dealing close!
Come one, come all to the {fair} at {place}: spices, wine and wares from beyond the sea, and the stalls buying dear.
By leave of the crown of {kingdom}, the {fair} is cried at {place}. Bring your goods and your purse!
market_dearth: Hear ye! {place} goes hungry: {good} fetches {pct}% over its worth. Whoever brings food will be paid well and blessed.
The criers of {kingdom} beg for {good}: {place} is in dearth and the poor queue at the bakers' doors.
Dearth in {place}! The granaries are low and {good} is dear. Let the carters make haste.
market_glut: Hear ye! The harvest is in at {place}, and {good} goes begging at {pct}% under its worth.
A bumper harvest at {place}: the barns are full and {good} is cheap as chaff. Buy now, sell in the lean weeks.
{place} cannot eat all its {good}: the criers call for buyers before it rots in the barns.
coronation: Hear ye! {ruler} is crowned in {kingdom}. Long may they reign!
By order of the crown of {kingdom}: {ruler} sits the throne, and all oaths are owed anew.
The bells of {kingdom} ring for {ruler}, crowned this week before the lords of the realm.
realm_fallen: Hear ye! The realm of {kingdom} is no more. Its banners are struck and its towns bow to new masters.
Mourn {kingdom}: its last walls have fallen and its crown is broken.
realm_restored: Hear ye! The banners of {kingdom} fly again over its old towns!
{kingdom} rises from its ashes. Let all who remember it rejoice.
peace: Hear ye! {kingdom} and {other} have made peace. Let the swords be sheathed and the roads reopen.
By treaty sealed: the war between {kingdom} and {other} is ended.
Peace between {kingdom} and {other}! The levies march home before the frost.
war: Hear ye! {kingdom} and {other} are at war. Every able man to his lord's banner!
War is declared between {kingdom} and {other}. Travellers, keep to the high roads.
saga_end: So ends {saga}. {title}. Let the tale be told in every hall.
revolt: Hear ye! {leader} and the lords with them rise against the crown of {kingdom}!
Rebellion in {kingdom}! {leader} raises banners against the throne.
revolt_end: Hear ye! The revolt in {kingdom} is ended. The realm is one again, for now.
The rebel banners in {kingdom} are lowered. The crown's peace returns.
rebellion: Hear ye! The common folk of {place} have risen against the lords of {kingdom}.
Unrest in {kingdom}: {place} is in open rebellion.
discovery: Hear ye! A new land is charted: {place}, found by {by}.
The map-makers add a new name: {place}, first sighted by {by}.
wonder: Hear ye! The {title} stands complete at {place}, raised by {by}!
A wonder for the ages: {by} has finished the {title} at {place}.
wonder_begun: Hear ye! {by} lays the first stone of the {title} at {place}.
Masons flock to {place}: {by} means to raise the {title}.
siege_won: Hear ye! {place} has fallen to {by} after {days} day(s) of siege.
{place} is taken! The siege laid by {by} is ended in victory.
siege_lost: Hear ye! The siege of {place} is broken. {by}'s host is driven off.
{place} holds! After {days} day(s), {by} gives up the siege.
lair_cleared: Hear ye! The outlaws of {place} are put down by {by}. {leader} will trouble the roads no more.
{place} is burned out! {by} has ended {leader} and the roads are safe again.
lair_risen: Beware! The outlaws of {place} under {leader} terrorise the country of {kingdom}. Travel in company.
A price is cried on {leader} of {place}, whose riders burn the villages of {kingdom}.
bank_failed: Hear ye! {bank} of {place} has shut its doors. Depositors are bidden to the receivers.
{bank} is broken! The strongrooms of {place} stand empty, and many a purse with them.
crown_default: Hear ye! The crown of {kingdom} will not pay its creditors. The bankers weep and the realm trembles.
By order of the crown, the debts of {kingdom} are repudiated. Let lenders beware.
coin_debased: Know all: the mint of {kingdom} strikes new coin of {purity} parts silver in the hundred. Prices rise in every market.
The coin of {kingdom} is clipped and thinned. Merchants weigh it twice and ask for more.
coin_recoinage: Hear ye! By edict of the crown of {kingdom}, all clipped coin is called in to the mint and struck anew at full weight. Bring your purses.
The crown of {kingdom} calls in its light coin ({purity} parts silver in the hundred) and strikes honest money again. There will be less of it about.
coin_shortage: Coin is short in {kingdom}: prices stand {pct}% under the world's, and the merchants cannot get paid in silver.
The criers of {kingdom} complain of want of coin. Goods are cheap there, {pct}% under the world's prices, for who has the silver to buy them?
coin_flood: Coin floods {kingdom}: every purse is full and every price {pct}% over the world's.
Silver runs like water in {kingdom}, and prices with it: {pct}% over the world's. Sell there, buy elsewhere.
tax_revolt: Hear ye! The people of {place} have driven out the tax collectors of {kingdom}. No coin will reach the crown from there this month.
Riot in {place}! The collectors of {kingdom} are stoned in the market and their ledgers burned.
tax_farm: Know all: the crown of {kingdom} has sold the taxes of {place} to {holder} for {amount}g. The farmer's men ride out tomorrow.
The taxes of {place} are farmed to {holder}. Its people bar their doors and hide their purses.
taxes_raised: By order of the crown of {kingdom}, the taxes are made {level}. Every hearth and every harvest shall pay more.
The crown of {kingdom} lays {level} taxes on land, hearth and market. The people grumble and count their coin.
army_unpaid: The soldiers of {kingdom} have gone three weeks without their pay. They sell their arms and drift home.
Mutiny in the camps of {kingdom}! The crown owes its army {amount}g and the captains will march no more.
offices_sold: Know all: judgeships and collectorships of {kingdom} are for sale ({amount}g raised). Their buyers mean to have it back.
The crown of {kingdom} sells its offices to whoever pays. Expect new fees at every gate and court.
crown_land_sold: The crown of {kingdom} sells royal manors to the great houses for {amount}g. Its own rents will be the less.
Hear ye! The demesne of {kingdom} is sold off piece by piece, and the lords grow fat on it.
caravan_taken: Hear ye! The {good} {carrier} bound for {place} was taken by {by} on the road from {from}. Expect dear {good} in {place}.
Ill news on the roads: {by} fell on the {good} {carrier} of {house} between {from} and {place}.
The {good} {carrier} to {place} never came in. {by} have it, and the stalls of {place} stand empty.

true: A merchant back from {fashionPlace} swears {fashionText}: {fashionGoods} are fetching a premium wherever the fashion has reached.
The pedlars say {fashionGoods} sell for twice their worth since the court at {fashionPlace} took them up.
false: They say the court at {fashionPlace} is sick of {fashionGoods} already. Nobody wants them now.
A drunk swears the new fashion is wooden shoes. Nobody believes him, but nobody knows better.

true: Bread in {kingdom} is up {pricePct}% since {sinceSeason}, the gazette says. Grain carters are doing well.
The gazette nailed up at the market says prices in {kingdom} are {pricePct}% above {sinceSeason}'s.
false: Prices are falling in {kingdom}, they say. The gazette must be wrong.
Some say bread will be cheap again by the next market day. Some say a lot of things.

true: {kingdom} and {enemy} are at each other's throats. The levies left last week.
A soldier home on leave says the war with {enemy} is going hard for {kingdom}.
false: Word is {kingdom} and {enemy} have signed a truce already.
A drover swears the war with {enemy} is over. He sounded very sure.

true: {blockader}'s ships hold the harbour mouth. Nothing sails out of {settlement} without their leave.
The fishers say {blockader}'s galleys sit off the coast day and night.
false: The blockade? Lifted, they say. {blockader}'s ships sailed home.
Someone swears the harbour is open again. Nobody has seen it with their own eyes.

true: {siegeTown} is under siege. The camp-followers say the stores won't last.
Smoke over {siegeTown} again. The siege goes on.
false: They say {siegeTown} opened its gates yesterday.
A tinker swears the siege of {siegeTown} was lifted days ago.

true: Talk is all of the {eventName} at {eventPlace}.
A carter just in from {eventPlace} says the {eventName} is real enough.
false: Someone swears the {eventName} at {eventPlace} is over already.
They say the {eventName} at {eventPlace} was never as bad as the criers made out.

true: Everyone is talking about {saga}. Nobody sleeps easy.
A pilgrim brought news of {saga}: it isn't over.
false: {saga}? Old wives' tales. It ended months ago, they say.
A bard swears {saga} is finished. Bards say a lot of things.

true: {rival} passed through here not long ago. {rivalNews}
You've just missed {rival}. They drank here and left a story behind.
false: {rival} is dead, they say. Fell off a cliff, or was it a horse?
Someone saw {rival} heading the other way entirely.

true: {ruler} wears the crown of {kingdom} now. {oldRuler} is gone.
New coins already, with {ruler}'s face on them.
false: They say {oldRuler} isn't dead at all, only hiding.
A pedlar swears {ruler} won't last the season. Who knows.

true: Lords are in revolt across {kingdom}. Choose your roads carefully.
The rebels hold towns in {kingdom}. Taxes go to whoever has the most spears.
false: The revolt? Bought off already, they say.
I heard the rebels in {kingdom} all surrendered. I heard wrong before.

true: The crier was here: {proclamation}
Did you hear the herald? {proclamation}
false: The crier said something about a crown, or a war. I was drinking.
A herald came through, but folk can't agree on what he said.

lines: They've called up every second son in {settlement} for the war with {enemy}.
War with {enemy}. Bread costs more and nobody knows when it ends.
My cousin marched off against {enemy} in the spring. Not a letter since.
If {enemy} comes this far, I'm taking the cart and the goats to the hills.
Every night the watch doubles. That's what war with {enemy} looks like from here.
Eyes open, stranger. We're at war with {enemy}, and spies come in all shapes.
Half the garrison went to the front against {enemy}. The rest of us sleep in our boots.
Captain says {enemy} scouts were seen two days out. Keep your blade handy.
The war with {enemy} has closed half my roads. Prices go up, and I can't help it.
Iron and horses sell themselves while {kingdom} fights {enemy}. Grain too.
I lost a whole wagon to {enemy} raiders last month. War is ruin for honest trade.
The lord's men took two of my oxen for the war against {enemy}. Who'll plough now?
War with {enemy}, and still the fields want sowing. Nobody fights a war on an empty belly.
They burn the fields first, the soldiers. Pray {enemy} never comes up this valley.
I bury the sons this war with {enemy} sends home. Pray for peace, traveller.
The shrine fills with mothers lighting candles for their boys at the front.
The crown wants more men for the war with {enemy}, and more silver. Always more silver.
A war with {enemy} is a fine thing for a family with ambitions. Ruinous for one without.
Spearheads, spearheads, spearheads. The war with {enemy} eats iron faster than I can forge it.
I haven't made a plough blade in weeks. The war with {enemy} wants swords.
I'm charging the crown double, and they pay it. That tells you how the war with {enemy} goes.
Lost my leg the last time {kingdom} fought {enemy}. A copper for an old soldier?
War makes beggars faster than any plague. Spare something?
My da says {enemy} soldiers eat children. Is that true?
We play knights and {enemy}. I'm always the knight!
I came the long way round. The roads near {enemy}'s border are crawling with patrols.
Saw a column marching to the front against {enemy}. Boys, most of them.
If they'd give me a spear I'd go myself. {enemy} needs a lesson.
Let {enemy} come. {settlement} has stood through worse.
I keep my head down and my door barred. Wars are for other people.
Best not to say too much about the war. You never know who's listening.
{kingdom} is at war with you, and you walk in here bold as brass?
The crown has put a price on your banners. I never saw you, understand?
Your war with {kingdom} has made you a lot of enemies here. Not me, mind. I sell to anyone.
{blockader}'s ships sit off the harbour. Nothing comes in and nothing goes out.
With the port shut by {blockader}, salt fish costs as much as beef.
The fishing boats stay tied up. {blockader}'s galleys sink anything that tries.
The blockade's strangling us. The harbour master drinks from noon now.
My cargo has sat on the quay for weeks. {blockader}'s blockade will ruin me.
Whatever you want from over the sea, it's dear. Blame {blockader}.
Smugglers still slip past {blockader}'s ships at night, if you know who to ask. I don't, of course.
My man fished for a living. Now he sits by the fire and curses {blockader}.
When the harbour's shut, the poor eat last.
You can see the smoke from {siegeTown} on a clear day. The siege goes on.
Refugees from {siegeTown} sleep in the barns. They say the walls won't hold much longer.
They're starving {siegeTown} out. I pray it never comes to that here.
Every cart that leaves for {siegeTown} comes back empty and bloody.
If {siegeTown} falls, we're next. The captain's had us drilling at dawn.
We've orders to turn back anyone fleeing {siegeTown} without papers. Grim work.
Bread for the siege camp at {siegeTown} sells at three times the price. War is good for someone.
I won't send a wagon near {siegeTown}. Both sides steal from carts.
Cold enough to freeze the ale in the barrel. Keep near the fire, traveller.
The passes are snowed shut. Nobody travels in winter if they can help it.
Wolves come close to the walls in winter. Mind the roads at dusk.
Spring at last. The roads are mud, but at least they're open.
Lambing season. Half the town hasn't slept in a week.
Summer's when the lords go to war. Dry roads, full granaries.
Long days and short tempers. Summer in {settlement} is always the same.
Harvest time! Every hand is in the fields, mine included.
Grain is cheap now. By spring it'll cost you dear. Buy while you can.
The harvest fair is coming. Best time of year in {settlement}.
The barley is in, thank the gods. Now to get it to the mill before the rain.
Good harvest or bad, the lord takes his share first.
Sowing time. If you've strong arms, there's work in the fields for a few coppers.
Pray for gentle rain. A wet spring and a dry summer, that's what we want.
There's no work in {settlement}. Half the men on my street stand at the corner from dawn to dusk.
The masters aren't hiring. If you've a job going, there's a dozen strong backs here would take it.
Idle hands, they say. Well, there's a lot of idle hands in {settlement} these days, and purses going missing.
Refugees, all over the square. Poor souls came with what they could carry.
We've folk sleeping in the church porch. They fled the fighting, they say. Bread's gone dearer since.
More mouths, same bread. The newcomers will work for anything, and the old hands don't like it.
The guilds have downed tools. Not a hammer in {settlement} till the masters pay a wage that buys bread.
Strike's on. The workshops are cold and the journeymen are in the taverns, singing rude songs about the masters.
Work for anyone who wants it in {settlement}. The workshops are hiring and the newcomers keep coming.
Good times. My cousin came in from the village last month and found a place the same week.
They've struck a new vein up in the hills. Half the lads in {settlement} have gone up with a pick.
A new mine, they say. More hands wanted, more mouths to feed, more coin in the taverns.
The mine's worked out. The miners are packing their carts; the smiths will pay through the nose for ore now.
Nothing left in those hills but holes. My brother dug there twenty years; now he's off to find work elsewhere.
The squire's hedged his fields for sheep. Where there were twenty hearths there's one shepherd and his dog.
Wool pays the lords better than tenants do. My uncle's family were turned out last spring; they went to the town.
They pulled the hedges down by night and drove the sheep into the river. The bailiff hasn't shown his face since.
A riot over the enclosures, and the sheriff's men out hunting the ringleaders. Bad times for honest folk.
The tenants rose over the rent. Beat the bailiff black and blue and sent him running back to town.
Rent riot out at the manor. When a landlord asks more than the land gives, this is what he gets.
The old lord left his manor to the Church. The monks keep the rents low, they say, but they never forget a tithe.
Our landlord's the abbey now, by the old lord's will. We'll see if prayers pay the rent.
The manor went with a bride to another house. New lord, new bailiff, same rent, I'll wager.
They married off the lord's daughter and the estate went with her. Nobody asked the tenants.
There's an estate going hereabouts. The old lord's in debt to his ears, they say.
New landlord on the manor. We'll see if he keeps the old rents or raises them.
The merchant's man came round with wool again. Spinning by the fire pays better than sitting idle all winter.
My wife weaves for a clothier now, piece by piece. The guild men grumble, but they don't come out to the villages.
In winter there's spinning to be had for the merchants. Come harvest, though, the wheel stands still.
Wool in the winter, the fields in the summer. That's how a family gets by out here.
A day's wage doesn't buy a day's bread any more. Something's got to give.
We work, and we still go hungry. My father says it wasn't like this in his day.
There's no {dearthGood} to be had in {settlement}, not for love nor money. Well, money, if you've a lot of it.
The stalls ran out of {dearthGood} days ago. The carters say the roads are bad.
{dearthGood}? You'll pay twice what it's worth here, if you find any at all.
Bring {dearthGood} to {settlement} and name your price. We've none.
Whoever hauls {dearthGood} in here this week will go home rich.
Everyone's short of {dearthGood}. The rich buy it all and the rest of us go without.
{settlement} is drowning in {glutGood}. You could buy a cartload for a song.
Too much {glutGood} and nobody to sell it to. Prices have fallen through the floor.
The {strikeGuild} has shut its doors. No {strikeGood} till the crown listens, they say.
Have you heard? The {strikeGuild} is out. You'll pay through the nose for {strikeGood} this week.
My cousin's in the {strikeGuild}. They'd sooner starve than work for what the stalls pay now.
With the {strikeGuild} out, anyone who brings {strikeGood} to {settlement} names his price.
Strikebreaking's a dangerous trade, friend. The {strikeGuild} remembers faces.
{glutGood} is cheap as dirt here. Carry it where they're short and you'll do well.
I can't shift my {glutGood}. Take some off my hands, cheap.
These are the lean weeks. The granary's near empty and the new crop's a long way off.
Everyone tightens their belt this time of year. Some have no belt left to tighten.
Bread's dear and getting dearer. The harvest can't come soon enough.
The lean season. Children cry at night here, and not from bad dreams.
Haven't eaten since yesterday. Anything, please. Anything at all.
The temple ran out of bread this morning. Have you a crust?
Food's the best trade in the lean weeks. Anyone who stored grain at harvest is rich now.
Sell me your grain and I'll pay you well. In the lean season everyone is hungry.
We're eating the seed corn now. That's how lean it is.
Old Hobb slaughtered his last pig to get through the lean weeks. Next year will be harder.
Plague at {eventPlace}. They've shut the gates there, and they burn the dead at night.
Keep your distance, stranger. They say the sickness at {eventPlace} spreads on the breath.
Vinegar on a cloth over your mouth. That's what the physicians say. For all the good it does.
Three carts of dead from {eventPlace} yesterday. I counted.
The plague at {eventPlace} is a judgement, some say. I say it is a sickness, and we must tend the sick.
I go to {eventPlace} tomorrow to give the last rites. Pray for me.
Herbs and remedies, very dear while the plague's at {eventPlace}. I won't apologise.
The granaries of {eventPlace} are bare. People are eating bark bread.
Hungry months. My neighbour sold his cow for a sack of oats.
If you have food to sell, sell it here. People are desperate.
Famine makes thieves of honest folk. Watch your packs.
Not a drop of rain in weeks. The wells around {eventPlace} are dry.
The river's so low you can walk across it. Bad for the mills, bad for the crops.
The priests pray for rain every morning. The sky ignores them.
The floods near {eventPlace} took whole villages. Mud up to the rooftops.
Don't take the low road. It's under water since the floods.
Bandits rule the roads near {eventPlace} now. Travel in company or not at all.
The bandit gang near {eventPlace} took a whole caravan. Killed the drivers.
The lord does nothing about the bandits. Maybe the lord is paid not to.
Pirates off {eventPlace}. No captain will sail without an escort.
Black sails near {eventPlace}. Three ships lost this month.
Gold near {eventPlace}! Half the young men left with picks and dreams.
My brother went prospecting at {eventPlace}. He came back with a cough and no gold.
The markets of {eventPlace} have crashed. Merchants hang themselves over their ledgers.
Nobody's buying. Nobody's selling. Coin's gone to ground since the crash.
Business is good! Caravans every day since trade picked up in {eventPlace}.
Never seen so many merchants on the roads. Good times, while they last.
Something big near {eventPlace}. Took three sheep and a shepherd.
They're offering silver for whoever kills the beast at {eventPlace}. No takers yet.
I heard it howling last night. Don't laugh, I heard it.
Did you see the comet? A sword of fire in the sky. Something terrible is coming, mark me.
The priests say the comet is an omen. They never say of what.
The sun went black at noon! I've never been so frightened in my life.
The ground shook near {eventPlace}. Walls fell, and the temple bell rang by itself.
Since the earthquake I sleep outside. Roofs fall, the sky doesn't.
A grand festival in {eventPlace}! Music and free ale, they say.
Everyone's off to the festival. I'm stuck minding the house.
Refugees pour into {eventPlace}. Poor souls, but where will they all sleep?
There's a new face on every corner since the refugees came. Some folk don't like it.
The blizzard buried the roads around {eventPlace}. Nobody's moving until the thaw.
Snow to the eaves. Two travellers froze on the road last night.
Best harvest in living memory around {eventPlace}! The granaries are bursting.
So much grain this year they're giving it to the pigs. Imagine!
The faithful are at each other's throats again. Schisms, crusades, I keep out of it.
The priests preach war from the pulpit now. That never ends well.
The lords are in revolt. Nobody knows who to pay taxes to any more.
Rebels hold the next town. If they come here, keep your mouth shut and your door barred.
Some say the rebels are right. I say nothing. Saying things gets you hanged.
A revolt is a dangerous game. Pick the winning side early, I always say.
My cousin rides with the rebels. I write to him every week, and to the crown every other week.
Nobody takes the road after dark now. Not with {leader}'s riders out of {lair}.
They hit a cart from {settlement} last week. Folk say it was the {lair} lot.
If the crown won't deal with {lair}, somebody should. There's a price on {leader}'s head, I hear.
My brother-in-law swears he saw smoke over {lair}. Bandits don't hide anymore, they build.
We'd clear out {lair} ourselves if the captain gave the word. He won't. Not enough of us.
Watch the roads, stranger. {leader} has eyes in every tavern from here to {lair}.
Lost two wagons on the road past {lair}. I pay guards now, and the guards cost more than the goods.
Go round {lair} if you value your purse. {leader} takes a toll in coin or in blood.
We ran the tax men out of town last week. They will be back with soldiers, mark me.
Not a penny more to the crown! Half the street said it, and the other half threw stones.
The crown sold our taxes to {bank}. Their bailiffs take twice what the king's men did.
A tax farmer's clerk came by with a ledger and two thugs. My hens are in his books now.
Land, hearth and market: the crown taxes them all, and heavier every season.
My cousin went over the border. Lighter taxes there, he says, and the bread's no dearer.
The garrison hasn't been paid in weeks. Half of them are selling their boots in the market.
Unpaid soldiers are worse than bandits. Lock your door tonight.
Bite the new coin and your teeth go through it. The crown's clipped it again.
Bread costs a third more than last year, and the baker swears it isn't his fault. It's the coin.
My grandmother's silver penny buys twice what the new ones do. I keep it under the floor.
I weigh every coin from {kingdom} twice now, and still lose on the exchange.
Prices in {settlement} are up, but so is everything I pay. Base coin makes fools of us all.
Another levy! The tax men took my second cow for the crown's war debts.
They say {ruler} owes the bankers more than the realm earns in a season. And who pays? We do.
The crown told the bankers it won't pay. Bold. Now nobody will lend to {kingdom} for a generation.
When kings don't pay their debts, why should anyone pay theirs? Mind you, the bailiffs still come for ours.
There's a crowd at the doors of {bank} since dawn, all waving their notes. I got out what I could.
They say {bank} can't pay out. If you've coin there, run, don't walk.
{bank} is broken. My savings with it. Thirty years at the loom, gone like smoke.
The receivers of {bank} pay a third of what's owed, they say, and take a year to do it.
Nobody has any coin. The baker takes eggs, the smith takes grain, and the tax man takes what's left.
Prices are low, aye, but what's the use when there's not a penny in the town to pay them with?
Goods are cheap in {kingdom} for want of coin. Bring silver and you can buy the market.
I sold on credit all season. The coin all went abroad to pay for the wine and the cloth.
So much silver about and still I can't afford a ham. Everything costs more every market day.
New coin everywhere, bright as the moon, and it buys less every week.
{kingdom} pays well for everything: the coin is cheap here. Sell here, buy in the lean realms.
The mines and the mint keep pouring out coin. Good for a seller, hard on a buyer.
They called in the old coin. I took ten clipped pennies to the mint and got nine good ones back. Honest money, they say.
The new coin rings true at last. Prices are coming down, though my purse is lighter for it.
My cousin put his savings in {listing}. Doubled in a month! I'm selling the mule to buy some.
Everyone's mad for {listing} at the Bourse. When the barber gives you tips on shares, sell.
{listing}'s shares aren't worth the paper now. My cousin's selling his mule back to me, at half.
They hanged a broker in effigy outside the Bourse. {listing} took half the town's savings with it.
The underwriters went bust. Every ship that sails from here now sails at its owner's risk.
{bank} won't pay the claims, they say. Insured! Ha. Insured against the insurers, that's what you'd need.
{bank} lends to kings and cobblers alike, at a price. Mind you pay it back. Their bailiffs don't knock twice.
Put your coin with {bank} if you've more than you can carry. Safer than under the bed, mostly.
Have you heard about {saga}? Everyone here talks of nothing else.
Strange times. {saga}, they're calling it. The old folk say it's like the stories.
My grandmother says {saga} is the end of the world. She said that about the last harvest too.
The wyrm! Burned a whole farmstead to ash near the peaks. You can see the scorch from the road.
The mountain shook and the wyrm came out. They say {villain}'s name in whispers.
Nobody grazes sheep on the high pastures any more. Not with the wyrm awake.
The Grey Cough. First you're tired, then you're coughing, then you're gone.
There's a scholar going about saying she can cure the Grey Cough. I hope she's right.
A lost heir, back from the dead? {villain}, he calls himself. Half the town believes him.
If the lost heir is real, there'll be war. If he's not, there'll be hangings.
This winter won't end. Frost in the fields well past when it should have thawed.
Bread riots in the next town over. The Long Winter, folk call it.
Black sails on the horizon. The reavers burned a fishing village not two days' sail from here.
{villain} leads the reavers, they say. A name to frighten children with.
There's a preacher splitting the faithful in two. Families won't sit at the same table.
Which side of the schism are you on? Careful how you answer here.
The Iron Company wasn't paid, so now they take what they're owed from us.
Sellswords with no master. {villain}'s men, they say. Lock up your daughters and your silver.
The comet grows redder every night. The prophets in the square say the end is near.
There's a cult now, worshipping the comet. Gave away all their goods. Fools.
{rival} was through here only days ago. Bought a round for the whole tavern.
You just missed {rival}! Same look in the eye as you, I'd say.
{rival} stayed a night and left before dawn. In a hurry to beat someone to something.
Everyone's talking about {rival}. You should do something worth talking about.
{rival} bought half my rope and all my torches. Off to some ruin, I suppose.
{rival} came through armed to the teeth. We watched that one closely. Same as you.
{rival} gave me a copper and showed me a real sword! Are you as famous as {rival}?
{oldRuler} is dead, and {ruler} wears the crown now. New ruler, new taxes, you'll see.
They rang the bells for {ruler} all day. I hope the new one is kinder than the old.
{ruler} on the throne. The coins with {oldRuler}'s face are still good, for now.
A new reign. Everyone's waiting to see which lords {ruler} favours.
The court is all a-flutter since {ruler} was crowned. Fortunes rise and fall in a day.
{ruler} hasn't yet named the new council. Every family in {kingdom} is scheming.
The crier was here: {proclamation}
A herald came through crying a coronation. A new crown, they say. Same old taxes.
Did you hear? {proclamation} I never thought I'd live to see it.
A whole realm gone. Kingdoms die like men, it seems.
Peace! The herald said so. {proclamation}
There's a treaty, the crier says. My boy might come home.
Peace, they say. I'll believe it when the soldiers are home and the taxes go down.
The crier was here yesterday. {proclamation}
War again, the herald says. It's always war again.
Did you hear the herald? {proclamation}
So that's over, then. The crier said as much. Folk will tell that tale for a hundred years.
The crier spoke of revolt. {proclamation}
A new land on the maps! {proclamation}
The herald says someone found an island no one knew. I'd like to see it, once.
Have you heard? {proclamation}
They say it can be seen from three days' ride. The crier tells it: {proclamation}
Stone and gold and a thousand masons. Folk will travel far to gape at it.
The herald brought news of a siege won. {proclamation}
Walls fall and banners change. The crier tells it like a song.
Did you hear the crier? {proclamation} Prices will climb, mark my words.
Embargoes, duties... the merchants grumble and the smugglers grin.
My cousin hauls salt over that border. Now he hauls it by night.
The herald says there's a trade treaty signed. {proclamation}
No more duties at the border, they say. The carters will be glad of it.
{proclamation} About time the crown thought of its own people.
Grain stays in the realm now, the crier says. The farmers near the border are furious.
Bad news from the crier: {proclamation}
A siege lost, the herald says. Somebody's sons won't come home.
You're the one who sacked {deedPlace}. I've heard the stories. Every one of them.
They say you burned {deedPlace} and took the coin from the temple. Is it true?
*steps back* Please, we've nothing worth taking here. Not like {deedPlace}.
You fed {deedPlace} through the hungry winter. People remember a thing like that.
The grain carts at {deedPlace} were yours, weren't they? Gods bless you for it.
My sister lives in {deedPlace}. She says your grain kept her children alive.
You pardoned that one at {deedPlace}. Mercy or weakness, folk can't agree.
A pardon at {deedPlace}! You've a soft heart, or a clever head.
You beat {deedVictim} in a duel near {deedPlace}! I'd have paid to see it.
They're saying you put {deedVictim} on their back. Was it a clean fight?
The duel near {deedPlace} is all anyone talks about. You've made a name, friend.
They say you faced down {deedVictim} out past {deedPlace}. Rather you than me.
Is it true about {deedVictim}? The hunters at {deedPlace} won't stop talking of it.
You're the one who saved {deedVictim} in the wilds near {deedPlace}. Good on you.
Word is you brought {deedVictim} in alive from out past {deedPlace}. Not everyone would have stopped.
Folk say you came back from the wilds by {deedPlace} with {deedVictim}. Lucky, or did you know where to dig?
Heard about {deedVictim}. Half of {deedPlace} will be out tramping the hills looking for more.
*grins* You and {deedVictim} of {deedPlace}, eh? Your spouse know about that?
Half the town's heard about you and {deedVictim}. The other half is pretending they haven't.
None of my business who you keep company with. Though {deedVictim}... really?
Have you heard? {scandalTale}
*lowers voice* {scandalTale} Don't say you heard it from me.
Everyone in {settlement} has a theory about {scandalSubject}. Mine's the worst, and I'd bet on it.
They're saying it started in {scandalPlace}. Smoke and fire, I say. About {scandalSubject}, there's always fire.
People will say anything about {scandalSubject}. I'll believe it when there's proof.
That talk about {scandalSubject}? Cruel, if it's a lie. Crueller if it isn't.
We've orders to box the ears of anyone repeating that tale about {scandalSubject}. So I've not heard it. Have you?
Captain says the talk about {scandalSubject} is treason. Captain also stopped smiling this week.
If {scandalSubject} really pawned the jewels, the coin's worth less tomorrow. I'm pricing it in today.
Crown debts. You hear that and you start asking to be paid in grain, not silver.
We are told to pray for {scandalSubject}'s soul. Some of us are praying harder than others.
An idol in the palace? The bishop has not slept since he heard.
Our lads bleed against {enemy} and the talk is {scandalSubject} is soft on them. You can feel the mood turning.
If it's true what they say of {scandalSubject}, the war with {enemy} is a farce. If it's false, someone should hang for saying it.
*goes pale* Y-yes, my lord. Whatever you need. Anything.
They say you hang men from the gate and leave them for the crows. I'll cause you no trouble.
Mothers frighten their children with your name. I didn't think you'd be so... ordinary-looking.
*bows low, trembling* We heard you were coming. The whole street went quiet.
Captain says to give you no cause for anger. Pass, my lord. Quickly.
I'll look the other way, my lord. I've a family.
*runs to hide behind a barrel*
Bless you, friend. Folk say you never pass a shrine without kneeling.
The gods favour you, they say. Would you say a prayer for my sick mother?
A pious soul in these hard times. You give me hope.
Your devotion is spoken of even in the high temple. Walk in the light, child.
Kneel with me a moment. It is rare to meet a lord who means the prayers.
You're the one who burns heretics, aren't you? I've always been very devout. Very.
Folk say you'd put a whole town to the torch for the faith. Is that holy?
I've heard what you do to people who cross you. I won't cross you.
*won't meet your eyes* Please, just tell me what you want.
You spared the beaten when you could have killed them. Not many lords would.
They say you've a kind heart. Kind hearts are rare these days.
You're the merciful one. My uncle owes you his life, he says.
They say you charge at the head of your men. The soldiers love you for it.
First into the fight, last out. That's what they sing about you.
*smirks* Not running away today, then?
The soldiers have a song about you. It's not a nice one.
An open hand, they say you have. The poor of {settlement} bless your name.
You bought the whole tavern a round last time. Folk haven't forgotten.
Counting coins again? They say you'd sell your mother for a good margin.
Hide the silver, here comes the miser. *laughs nervously* Only joking.
It's you! My children will never believe I spoke to you!
The whole town loves you, you know. We'd follow you anywhere.
Kinslayer. *spits* The gods will have their due from you.
Your own blood. How do you sleep at night?
The champion of the lists! I won a silver on you at the last tourney.
Will you be riding in the next tournament? The whole town would come.
Tavern's that way, if you're looking. You usually are, they say.
*sniffs* Started early today?
A sea wolf, they call you. The salt's in your blood, I can tell.
They say you've read every book in three kingdoms. Can you read this letter for me?
The merchant prince himself! Half the caravans on these roads carry your goods.
They say you could buy {settlement} twice over. Could you?
Your word's good as gold, folk say. Rare in a lord.
Silver-tongued, they call you. I'll count my change twice, if it's all the same.
Back on the road again? You've seen more of the world than anyone in {settlement}.
They say you're always three moves ahead. I'll keep my secrets to myself, then.
Fancy a game of dice? No? They say you never refuse.
That scar... I've heard the story. Was it really a bear?
They say you judge with mercy. My brother's in a debtors' cell. Would you hear his case?
A merciful lord. Folk go to your court hoping, not trembling.
Your court hangs thieves by the dozen, they say. I've never stolen a thing in my life.
Hard justice at your court, folk say. Hard, but the roads are safer.
The gallows at your seat are never empty, I hear.
A fair judge, they call you. The poor get a hearing at your court as well as the rich.
If I've a quarrel with my neighbour, I'd want you to hear it.
Your court favours the temples, they say. The priests sing your praises.
A lord who listens to the clergy. My mother would approve.
Your court opens its purse to petitioners, they say. Is it true?
Folk say you never send a hungry man away from your hall.
*drops to one knee* Your Majesty! In {settlement}! Nobody told us!
Long live the crown! Forgive me, Majesty, I didn't recognise you at first.
Your Majesty. The taxes are heavy, if I may say so. Only if I may.
The king, here, in the street! Wait till I tell my wife.
Majesty. My family has always been loyal, whatever you may have heard.
*snaps to attention* Your Majesty! The watch is at your command!
A foreign crown, walking our streets. The lords here will want to know why.
You're a king, they say. Not ours, though. Mind that.
You're the one pressing a claim to the throne! Bold. Maybe mad.
Folk are choosing sides in your war for the crown. I choose to keep my head.
If you win, remember {settlement} was kind to you. If you lose, we never met.
An exile, they say. A crown lost. That's a hard road.
You had a throne in your grasp once. Now look at you.
Exiles come through here sometimes. Most never go home.
{house}! My father spoke of your father. Or was it your grandfather?
An old name, {house}. Folk here remember it.
The {house} line goes on, I see. Good. The world needs old families.
{house} has been in the songs for generations. And here's another of you!
Three generations of {house}, and the name only grows.
{house} is the talk of every hall. Mind the envy that comes with that.
Every noble family wants a marriage with {house} these days. So my mistress says.
There's something cold about you. The dogs won't stop barking.
Folk cross the street when you pass. I'd guess you know why.
Are you really {player}? The {player}? Can I touch your sword?
Your name's known three kingdoms over, {player}. I heard it in a tavern by the sea.
You're {player}, aren't you? My cousin swore you passed through {settlement} once.
Folk in {kingdom} have started saying your name, {player}. Not loudly, yet.
They drink your health in every alehouse in {kingdom}, {player}.
My boy plays at being {player} with a stick for a sword. You've a following here.
For you, {player}, a fair price. Folk will buy from me just to say you did.
There's a song about you, {player}. Half of it's lies, but I'd wager the best half's true.
Grandchildren will hear how {player} came to {settlement}. I'll make sure of it.
Every house in {kingdom} would give a daughter's dowry to dine with {house}. And here you are.
I've heard what folk say of you, {player}. I'll count my change twice.
There are stories about you in {kingdom}. None of them make me want to stand close.
Mothers call their children in when you walk by, {player}.
The watch has your face drawn on a board by the gate. Did you know?
I'm to keep an eye on you while you're in {settlement}. Orders. Don't make it interesting.
{rivalHouse} holds sway in {kingdom}, and they've no love for {house}. Folk here know it.
You'll find doors shut here, friend. {rivalHouse} pays well to keep them that way against {house}.
Everyone in {settlement} knows {rivalHouse} and {house} are at each other's throats.
My lord's kin are of {rivalHouse}. I'd not linger in {kingdom}, were I of {house}.
Bread is dear in {kingdom}: up {pricePct}% since {sinceSeason}. My children eat porridge twice a day now.
A loaf costs what a pie did in {sinceSeason}. {pricePct}% more, the baker says, and he's not lying.
Food's {pricePct}% dearer than in {sinceSeason}. Bring grain to {kingdom} and you'll sell it before you unload.
Grain's fetching {pricePct}% more than in {sinceSeason}. A cart from a glutted town would pay for itself twice.
I've never seen bread so dear in {kingdom}. Whoever's sitting on a granary is a rich man this season.
Linen's cheaper than it's been in years. Every cottage has a loom going.
You can't sell linen for what the flax cost. The cottagers weave it faster than folk can wear it out.
The grain dealers are buying up every sack against a bad harvest. They'll sell it back to us at twice the price come spring.
Engrossers, the lot of them. Lofts full of grain while the baker can't get flour. The crown should throw them open.
Word is the dealers have been hoarding grain. If the crown has any sense it'll forbid it before the hungry months.
Everything costs {pricePct}% more than in {sinceSeason}. My wages don't.
Prices in {kingdom} are up {pricePct}% since {sinceSeason}. Buy today, for tomorrow it costs more.
{pricePct}% dearer than in {sinceSeason}, and they tell us the coin is sound.
Bread's cheap in {kingdom} this season. The farmers grumble, everyone else eats.
Food has never been so cheap. A good year, or a glut: depends whether you grow it or eat it.
The pass is shut with snow. Nothing comes over the mountains till the thaw, and you can taste it in the prices.
Two carters turned back at the pass yesterday. Drifts to the axles, they said.
The flood took the bridge clean away. Now it's the ferryman's fare or wet boots.
Since the bridge went, the carts queue at the water. Someone ought to build it again, and charge for it too.
The road's a ruin: ruts to your knees, holes to break an axle. The crown's road-money goes elsewhere, it seems.
Takes a day longer to the next town than it did. Nobody mends the road any more.
Spring mud. The carts sink to the hubs on the old track; wait a fortnight if you can.
Everything comes slow in the thaw. The roads are soup.
Paved all the way now. A wagon makes the next town before noon.
The new highway's brought the merchants. Prices are fairer since: what's dear here is cheap there no longer.
The barges come up the canal every morning. Stone, grain, fish still fresh: that's what water does.
Since they dug the canal the carters have little work, but bread's cheaper.
There's a toll on the bridge now. Pay it or wade, and the river's cold.
Tolls, tolls. Every cartload pays at the gate, and the price of everything goes up a copper.
The road gangs are hiring. Good wages, hard work, stone to haul.
Masons everywhere this season. The quarry can't cut stone fast enough; it's dear as anything.
Have you seen the fields? Half the ears are empty. It'll be a thin harvest this year, mark me.
No rain when we wanted it, rain when we didn't. The crop is poor; buy your flour now, while it's cheap.
The reeve walked the fields and came back grey. Bread will be dear by spring.
Never seen the wheat stand so tall. There'll be grain to spare this autumn, and cheap.
A fat year coming. The farmers say the barns won't hold it all.
Rust in the wheat, red as a fox. The whole valley's got it.
They're burning the blighted fields out past the mill. The smoke's been up for days.
Locusts! A cloud of them came over the ridge and ate the barley to the ground.
You can hear them at night, chewing. By morning there's nothing green left.
Murrain among the cattle. The herdsmen are burning carcasses on the common.
Half my neighbour's sheep dead in a week. Meat will be dear, and wool.
A poor harvest, and the winter not yet begun. Folk are counting every loaf.
The granary's half empty already. Pray the spring comes early.
A rich harvest this year. Bread's cheap and the ale's flowing.
Barns full to the rafters. The farmers complain grain fetches nothing, but nobody goes hungry.
Have you heard? At {fashionPlace}, {fashionText}. Every lady wants {fashionGoods} now.
So they say at {fashionPlace}: {fashionText}. The merchants can't get {fashionGoods} fast enough.
The fashion from {fashionPlace} is for {fashionGoods}. Sell them here and name your price.
One must have {fashionGoods} this season. At {fashionPlace} {fashionText}, and I will not be thought provincial.
Everyone at {fashionPlace} wants {fashionGoods}. I paid twice their worth and was glad of it.
If you deal in {fashionGoods}, the courts will pay a premium until the fashion passes. It always passes.

patronage._comment: Patronage & Great Works (src/systems/patronage.js). Clients (artists, scholars, architects, physicians, chroniclers) are offered in a town's salon, chosen by a hash of the world seed, the town and the month (no RNG). They draw a weekly stipend, produce works on commission and can be poached by rival Houses or leave when unpaid or idle. Great Works are multi-stage projects at a settlement the player rules or holds a house in: each stage wants goods + gold delivered, then days of paid labour. Every effect key has a reader: research (Technology.getResearchBonus), conversion (PlayerReligion.conversionMultiplier), education (Upbringing growth), vision (Player.updateVisibility), festivalRenown (Festivals.getReputation), riverCross (Infrastructure.getRiverPenalty), care/woundHeal (Ailments), mood (Taxation happiness target via settlement.patronage), monthlyPrestige (House Prestige, paid by Patronage). Kingdoms build wonders too (npc*), first to finish a unique work claims it for the world.
